title: Linear-regression gradient descent
description: Derive, calculate and verify one simultaneous training step.

pages.title: Use error to choose a better line
pages.subtitle: Continue Lesson01. A gradient tells us how cost changes when a parameter changes.
blocks: Data: (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5). Initial intercept theta 0 = 0; slope theta 1 = 1.
A partial derivative holds the other parameter fixed. Read dJ/dtheta as the sensitivity of cost to a small parameter increase.
Alpha is the learning rate: it scales the size of our parameter step.

pages.title: Derive the intercept gradient
pages.subtitle: Every prediction increases by 1 when the intercept increases by 1.
blocks: The derivative of a square gives 2r. That 2 cancels the 1/2 in the cost. The remaining gradient is the mean signed residual.

pages.title: Derive the slope gradient
pages.subtitle: A slope change affects a prediction in proportion to that example's input.
blocks: For x = 3, increasing the slope by 0.01 increases the prediction by 0.03.
Same residuals, different influence: multiply each residual by its own input before averaging.
These are the two gradients in Lecture 1, PDF page 44. Do not square residuals again when calculating them.

pages.title: Substitute all three examples
pages.subtitle: Both gradients use the same old parameters, before any update.
blocks: g is a short name for the gradient value. A negative gradient suggests a small increase in that parameter will lower cost.

pages.title: Update both parameters together
pages.subtitle: Lecture 1, page 41: calculate temporary values, then replace both parameters.
blocks: Subtracting a negative number increases the parameter. Both the intercept and the slope rise in this example.
Do not replace the intercept and then recalculate the slope gradient. That would mix old and new states.

pages.title: Predict again with the new line
pages.subtitle: Keep exact fractions until the final decimal to avoid rounding drift.
blocks: The predictions are approximately 1.433333, 2.733333 and 4.033333. They are all closer to their targets than before.

pages.title: Check that the cost really decreased
pages.subtitle: A useful update must be checked using new predictions, not old residuals.
blocks: One full-batch step uses all 3 examples and makes one simultaneous update.
A negative gradient is a local direction clue. An excessively large learning rate can still overshoot and increase cost.

pages.title: Your turn: one step from another line
pages.subtitle: Use the same data, but begin at intercept 1 and slope 1.
blocks: 1. Predict all three targets and calculate signed residuals.
2. Calculate both mean gradients.
3. Update the intercept and slope simultaneously.
4. Recompute the predictions and half-MSE. Did the cost decrease?
Write the old and new parameter values in separate columns.

pages.title: Practice answer: gradients and update
pages.subtitle: First finish all old-state calculations; then change the parameters.
blocks: Initial practice cost: (0 + 0 + 1) / 6 = 1/6.

pages.title: Practice answer: verify the new cost
pages.subtitle: Two predictions now overshoot, but the overall fit improves.
blocks: This is below 1/6. Improving average loss does not require every example to improve.
Avoid: reversed residual signs; averaging twice; updating one parameter before computing the other gradient.
